classification.difficultyReason: Follow the drawn rectangle/triangle dissection, then produce a contrasting leaning trapezium where the illustrated internal cuts fail; short property-based counterexample.

content.prompt: Here is yet another way of dissecting a trapezium to find its area. Cut the two triangles from the end of the trapezium and rearrange them to form a rectangle and a triangle, as shown below.

spec.description: Complete actual source givens, perpendicular heights/equality families and mathematical shaded regions retained. Native editable black10pt figure, no derived dimensions.

children.label: a
children.prompt: What is the value of L?

answer.worked: The two end triangles have combined base $L=17-6=11$ cm.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the area of the trapezium.

answer.worked: The rectangle area is $6(8)=48\text{ cm}^2$, and the triangle area is $\tfrac12(11)(8)=44\text{ cm}^2$. Their total is $48+44=92\text{ cm}^2$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Can you draw a trapezium in which this method of dissection will not work?

answer.short: Yes; draw a strongly leaning trapezium, so one vertical cut falls outside the shape.
answer.worked: For example take bottom vertices (0,0),(5,0) and top vertices (4,2),(7,2). The bases are parallel, with an obtuse bottom-right angle and obtuse top-left angle. The perpendicular from (7,2) lands outside the bottom segment; the two internal end-triangle cuts pictured in the question cannot both be made.
